strengths: Addresses a highly practical and important problem: enabling LRMs to maintain input-output language consistency in multilingual settings
Strong empirical results: achieves ~99% language consistency on in-domain languages and LC&Acc scores of 36.88% (1.5B) and 62.24% (7B) across all languages
Comprehensive experimental design with multiple strong baselines (Prompt-Control, DIT, QRT, Naive-RL, SLC-RL) and thorough ablation studies demonstrating contribution of each component
Novel CTA reward design that cleverly uses self-generated English reasoning as a teacher to align multilingual reasoning, avoiding external model dependencies for gap estimation
Insightful generalization analysis (Section 5.3) revealing that language family similarity drives transfer learning, with actionable implications
Rigorous evaluation methodology with 4 runs, macro-averaging, and validation on two benchmarks (MMATH and PolyMath)
Well-documented reproducibility details including hyperparameters, implementation settings, and judge instructions in appendices
weaknesses: Moderate novelty over concurrent work: LC reward is an incremental strictening of existing soft consistency rewards (Park et al. 2025); lacks direct experimental comparison with concurrent methods (Park et al. 2025, Hwang et al. 2025, Lee et al. 2025)

Critical reproducibility concern: CTA reward depends on DeepSeek-V3-0324 which may be unavailable or expensive; Table 4 shows significant degradation with alternative judge (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: 32.91% vs 36.88%), indicating fragile reproducibility
Limited scope: only 5 in-domain languages, small models (1.5B/7B), restricted to math reasoning domain; generalization to other tasks and language families unclear
Language detection dependency: LC reward relies on langdetect library without comparison to alternatives (xlm-roberta, Cld3, FastText); potential systematic error source not explored

Incomplete analysis of performance anomalies: Arabic OOD shows unexplained LC drop (33.31% Iter-1 → 11.03% Iter-2); some languages show surprisingly poor generalization despite strong in-domain performance; no error analysis or case studies
Lack of statistical rigor: four runs mentioned but no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests provided; macro-averaging can obscure language-specific failures
Severe generalization limitations revealed in Table 5: Korean (isolate language) achieves 0.0% when trained on fr/ja, suggesting the approach fails for novel language families
Judge instruction design not ablated: the CTA judge prompt (Appendix A) is critical but lacks sensitivity analysis; no exploration of alternative alignment metrics
Data filtering bias not analyzed: cold-start SFT filters by LC&Acc scores without characterizing what is filtered and whether this biases toward certain problem types
Binary LC reward may cause optimization issues (sparse gradients); no exploration of soft LC variants or comparison justifying why binary is superior beyond empirical results

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: language consistency and multilingual reasoning performance gaps in LRMs
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 10 languages, 2 model sizes, and 2 benchmarks with multiple runs and macro-averaging
Achieves dramatic improvements in language consistency (nearly 100% for in-domain languages), directly addressing the stated goal
Thorough ablation studies and analysis (Tables 3-5) providing useful insights into reward components and language family generalization
Clear methodology and well-structured presentation of the training procedure (Algorithm 1) and reward formulations
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Primarily combines existing techniques (GRPO, binary language detection for LC reward, LLM-as-Judge for CTA reward) without significant algorithmic innovation

Brittle LC reward design: Relies on langdetect library (known robustness issues), uses binary reward (0 vs -1) with no partial credit, and creates evaluation circularity (same tool for training and evaluation)

Questionable CTA reward premises: Assumes English reasoning is always superior (linguistically debatable) and shows high sensitivity to judge model choice (32.91% vs 36.88% performance spread with different judges)
Restricted experimental scope: Only 5 in-domain languages with 3K samples each, 2 RL iterations (due to time constraints), and model sizes limited to 1.5B/7B (GPU constraints)
Overstated trade-off resolution: While LC improves dramatically, accuracy degrades significantly in some cases (M-Thinker-1.5B Iter-1 Acc: 35.59% vs Naive-RL: 49.99%, a 14% drop on ID-AVG)
Mixed OOD generalization: Dramatic performance drops for certain languages (Arabic LC drops to 33.31%), and post-hoc language-family explanations lack rigorous validation
Heavy dependence on proprietary models: DeepSeek-V3 for judging, DeepSeek-R1 for data generation; no code release mentioned; severely limits reproducibility
Missing statistical rigor: Multiple runs conducted but no standard deviations or significance testing reported; confidence intervals would strengthen claims
Incomplete baseline comparisons: No comparison with other recent concurrent multilingual reasoning work (Park et al. 2025, Hwang et al. 2025); DeepSeek-R1-0528 only shown in separate table
No qualitative analysis: Missing error cases, failure modes, or example outputs contrasting M-Thinker with baselines
Evaluation circularity risk: Using langdetect for both reward signal and LC metric evaluation masks potential detection failures
Post-hoc generalization analysis: Table 5 language-family patterns are explained after results rather than validated through targeted experiments

strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem affecting global LRM deployment with clear motivation and compelling examples
Novel CTA (Cross-lingual Thinking Alignment) reward elegantly uses the model's own English reasoning as a teacher for knowledge transfer, demonstrating technical insight
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across two benchmarks (MMATH, PolyMath) with 10 languages covering diverse language families, multiple runs, and well-designed in-domain/out-of-domain splits
Strong empirical results achieving ~100% language consistency for in-domain languages while maintaining competitive accuracy (LC&Acc nearly equals backbone Acc in input language)
Extensive ablations (Tables 3, 8) and analysis demonstrating contribution of each component; generalization study revealing language-family effects provides valuable insights for future work
Excellent reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, training procedures (Algorithm 1), data construction details, and GPU configurations
Systematic training pipeline (cold-start SFT, rejection sampling, iterative GRPO) is well-motivated and clearly presented
weaknesses: Scope significantly limited: only 5 training languages and evaluation restricted to mathematical reasoning; unclear whether approach generalizes to code generation or other reasoning types, limiting broader impact claims

Critical unresolved failure case: Arabic shows dramatic LC degradation in out-of-domain setting (33.31%→11.03%) contradicting claims of 'excellent generalization,' with insufficient error analysis or explanation (script differences? language family? translation artifacts?)

CTA reward introduces computational cost and noise: DeepSeek-V3 querying required per example; Table 4 shows sensitivity (Qwen2.5 judge drops to 32.91%, below w/o Rcta baseline of 34.43%), raising reproducibility concerns with external proprietary model dependency

Language detection reliability not adequately addressed: LC reward depends on langdetect library with acknowledged limitations; alternative tools deferred to future work despite being foundational to a paper on language consistency

Technical novelty is moderate: LC reward is a simple binary penalty, CTA uses standard LLM-as-a-Judge, training combines existing techniques; contribution is primarily the application rather than algorithmic innovation

Methodological choices lack justification: rejection sampling criterion ('0 < |O_correct| < N') for 'hard' examples undefined; cold-start SFT filtering by LC&Acc score risks selection bias; multilingual data via machine translation without human validation

Incomplete analysis of consistency-accuracy trade-off: claims to 'almost overcome' trade-off but evidence is mixed; some languages show accuracy degradation with LC enforcement; w/o Rlc ablation reveals cases where relaxing consistency improves accuracy
Limited RL iterations (only 2 due to time constraints) raises questions about convergence; unclear if further improvements possible with more iterations

Missing critical analyses: no qualitative reasoning examples, error analysis of remaining inconsistencies, or explanation of why English provides better reasoning baseline (pretraining balance? corpus composition? script effects?)

Computational overhead underexplored in main text: training uses 8×8 H20 GPUs + 2×8 for rewards; this substantial resource requirement deserves prominence in limitations given reproducibility concerns

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 3 model sizes, 10 languages, and 2 benchmarks with consistent strong results (near 100% language consistency, 63.25% LC&Acc vs 45.01% SLC-RL baseline)
Well-motivated problem addressing genuine multilingual reasoning limitations in current LRMs with clear practical importance for global deployment
Thorough ablation studies and analysis including human evaluation (0.88 Pearson correlation), generalization patterns by language family, and hard vs. soft reward tradeoffs
Systematic training procedure incorporating cold-start SFT, rejection sampling, and iterative RL with detailed implementation details supporting reproducibility
Meaningful empirical insights about model-size dependent tradeoffs (hard LC works for 7B but causes accuracy drops on 1.5B) and cross-lingual transfer patterns
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: LC reward is straightforward binary language detection, CTA reward applies existing LLM-as-Judge paradigm, core GRPO algorithm from concurrent work; main contribution is engineering combination

Critical dependency on fragile components: langdetect library reliability for code-switching and low-resource languages not evaluated; acknowledged but unaddressed failure modes on extremely low-resource languages
Significant practical limitations: CTA reward requires external LLM (DeepSeek-V3) during training with 2×8 additional GPUs; not practical for many users; no computational cost-benefit analysis
Limited evaluation scope: only 5 training languages and 3K samples per language; exclusively math reasoning domain tested; unclear generalization to other tasks or underrepresented language families

Incomplete trade-off analysis: LC&Acc metric obscures fundamental accuracy-consistency tradeoff; for 1.5B model hard LC degrades accuracy substantially (35.78% vs 47.98%), limiting practical deployment
Generalization study limited to 2 training languages; shows 0.0 generalization to Korean without investigation; language-family claims partially predictable and not linguistically rigorous
Small-scale human evaluation: only 30 samples per language testing alignment ratios, not end-to-end reasoning quality; limited validation of whether forced alignment preserves reasoning faithfulness

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: input-output language consistency in multilingual reasoning models, with clear motivation and real-world relevance

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple dimensions: three model sizes (1.5B, 4B, 7B), two benchmarks (MMATH, PolyMath), 10 languages, multiple metrics (LC, Acc, LC&Acc, DW-ACC), and diverse baselines

Thorough ablation studies (Table 3) effectively isolate contributions of each component; additional analyses include human evaluation of CTA reward (Pearson ρ=0.88), judge model comparison, and language family-aware generalization
Strong empirical achievement on language consistency: achieves ~100% LC on in-domain languages while maintaining reasonable accuracy, representing meaningful improvement over baselines
Clear methodology with detailed descriptions (Algorithm 1), comprehensive implementation details, and commitment to release code/models/data for reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: the approach combines existing techniques (GRPO, langdetect library, LLM-as-Judge) without substantial methodological innovation. LC reward is straightforward application of language detection; CTA is basic pattern matching on intermediate results. This is primarily an engineering contribution rather than fundamental research advance

Critical unvalidated assumption: multilingual training questions are machine-translated via DeepSeek-V3 with no validation of translation quality, naturalness, or fidelity to original problem structure. This is a major confound that could undermine claims about genuine multilingual reasoning capability

Unclear necessity of CTA reward: ablation (Table 3) shows CTA provides only ~3.8 point accuracy improvement on 1.5B model while adding substantial computational overhead from judge model calls. Heavy dependence on expensive DeepSeek-V3 (or degradation with smaller models) weakens the contribution's practical utility and reproducibility

Inconsistent and concerning accuracy results: Japanese (ja) shows regression in Iter-2 (60.56% vs baseline 53.44%), and Arabic (ar) OOD performance collapses from 84.68% to 75.12% between iterations, suggesting overfitting to training languages or training instability that contradicts robustness claims

Overstated generalization claims: language family analysis (Table 5) uses only 2 training languages on 1.5B model; Korean→all languages shows 0.00% transfer. OOD performance is highly inconsistent across languages, contradicting narratives of effective generalization; the mechanism of why English alignment should transfer across language families is unexplained

Severe judge model dependency: results are best with proprietary DeepSeek-V3-0324; smaller models degrade performance; acknowledged failure on extremely low-resource languages. This creates reproducibility barriers and introduces a single point of quality failure, with no discussion of computational overhead from repeated judge calls during training

Limited experimental scope: only mathematical reasoning evaluated (MMATH/PolyMath); generalization to code, logic, or other reasoning domains is speculative. Only 5 training languages, 3K samples per language, 2 RL iterations—all limited by acknowledged resource constraints but still narrow

Missing key comparisons: related concurrent work (CM-Align/Zhang et al. 2025b, Park et al. 2025, Hwang et al. 2025) is cited but not empirically compared, leaving unclear how this work differs in practice

Fragile language detection: langdetect may struggle with code-text mixing, mathematical notation, and low-resource languages. Acknowledged alternatives (XLM-RoBERTa, CLD3, FastText) are untested, representing unexamined confounds

No statistical significance testing: four evaluations averaged without error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite accuracy improvements of 3-8 points that may fall within noise margins

strengths: Addresses important practical problem: language inconsistency and poor multilingual performance in LRMs; well-motivated and timely
Strong empirical results: achieves ~99% language consistency on in-domain languages while maintaining accuracy (63.32% LC&Acc vs. 43.14% for SLC-RL baseline on 7B)
Clear and principled methodology: strict LC reward and intuitive CTA reward using LLM-as-Judge; well-justified design choices including use of self-generated English paths
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 10 languages across diverse families, 3 model sizes, 2 benchmarks (MMATH and PolyMath), strong baselines including prompt-based, SFT, and soft LC approaches
Thorough ablation studies: individual reward contributions tested, multiple judge models evaluated, human evaluation validates LLM judge (Pearson r=0.88), generalization analysis per language
Excellent reproducibility: detailed training procedure (Algorithm 1), comprehensive implementation details in appendices, promises to release code/models/data with badges shown
Good generalization to out-of-domain languages: 94.64% LC consistency on OOD for 7B Iter-1, revealing meaningful cross-lingual pattern learning rather than task-specific hacks
Insightful analysis: generalization study (Table 5) shows language family effects, explaining better transfer within Indo-European or Sino-Tibetan language groups
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scope: only 5 in-domain and 5 out-of-domain languages; MMATH has only 374 problems (≈37 per language, ≈9 per difficulty level); no statistical significance testing despite small sample sizes; lacks evaluation on other reasoning tasks beyond math

Unexplained performance gap on PolyMath: 26 percentage point drop in LC&Acc compared to MMATH (32.37% vs 58.45% for 7B Iter-1); suggests potential benchmark-specific overfitting or method limitations not discussed

Hard LC reward hurts smaller models: Table 10 shows hard LC decreases 1.5B accuracy to 31.72% vs 46.80% with soft LC; undermines generalizability claims and raises concerns for practitioners deploying smaller models
CTA reward computational overhead: requires external LLM judge (DeepSeek-V3) for every sample, doubling training cost; cost-effectiveness trade-offs and scalability concerns not fully explored

Cold-start SFT data quality concerns: multilingual responses generated by DeepSeek-R1 (which itself struggles with task), filtered by LC&Acc without reporting rejection rates; potential circularity in training on data from model that fails at target task

Rejection sampling bias: selects 'hard' questions with 0 < |O_correct| < N, excluding very confident/uncertain cases; bias impact not analyzed; N=8 sampling is small with unexamined statistical properties
Incomplete comparison with concurrent work: Park et al., Hwang et al., Lee et al. cited but not included in empirical comparisons; limits assessment against alternative solutions
Requiring parallel English questions: Algorithm 1 assumes parallel English for each multilingual question; reduces practical applicability when parallel data unavailable
Limited RL iterations: only 2 iterations due to resource constraints; unknown if performance would improve further, affecting optimization quality claims

Low-resource language support deferred: CTA reward fails for extremely low-resource languages where judge models cannot comprehend input; fallback strategies (Format+Acc+LC) not tested; limits practical applicability
